NUS ST4231 — Computer Intensive Statistical Methods¶

A systematic case study using the Palmer Penguins dataset¶

Central question:

How can we use computation to perform statistical estimation, uncertainty quantification, latent-variable inference, and posterior simulation when an analytic solution is difficult, inefficient, or unavailable?

This notebook is designed as a tutor-style case study, not merely a collection of functions. Every major method is approached in the same sequence:

  1. Statistical question — what are we trying to learn?
  2. Mathematical idea — what identity makes the computation possible?
  3. Algorithm — how do we turn the idea into steps?
  4. Implementation — preferably from scratch rather than as a black box.
  5. Diagnostics — how do we know the computation is trustworthy?
  6. Tuning / trade-offs — what changes efficiency or stability?
  7. Failure mode — how can the method go wrong?
  8. Interpretation — what does the output mean statistically?

Dataset¶

We use the Palmer Penguins data. It contains measurements on three penguin species—Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo—including bill dimensions, flipper length, body mass, sex, island, and year.

Original data credit: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014), Palmer Station LTER. The palmerpenguins project makes the cleaned data openly available.

  • Project: https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/
  • CSV mirror used by this notebook: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv

ST4231 concepts covered¶

Part Concept Main role in computational statistics
A Random variate generation Turn uniform pseudo-randomness into useful distributions
B Monte Carlo integration Replace difficult expectations/integrals by sample averages
C Variance reduction Obtain more precision from the same computational budget
D EM algorithm Fit latent-variable / missing-data models iteratively
E Markov chains Build stochastic dynamics with a desired long-run distribution
F Metropolis–Hastings Sample from a target known only up to proportionality
G Gibbs sampling Sample multivariate posteriors through full conditionals
H Bootstrap Approximate sampling distributions by resampling the data
I Jackknife Approximate bias/variance by systematic deletion
J Empirical likelihood Likelihood-style inference without a parametric distribution

The notebook intentionally includes validation against known answers wherever possible. A computational method is much easier to trust when we can make it recover a quantity that we already know in a controlled setting.

0. Setup, reproducibility, and numerical conventions¶

Computer-intensive statistics is especially sensitive to implementation details. We therefore make several choices explicit:

  • numpy.random.default_rng is used instead of global random state.
  • Random seeds are fixed for reproducibility.
  • Probabilities are often computed on the log scale to avoid underflow.
  • Covariance matrices receive a small diagonal regularizer when inverted.
  • Monte Carlo algorithms report uncertainty or effective sample size rather than only a point estimate.
  • Bokeh is used for all visualisations.

0.1 A small helper for explanatory tables¶

Throughout the notebook, tables are not treated as decoration. Each table is followed by an interpretation because a numerical result is only useful if we can connect it back to the statistical question.

In [2]:
def tidy_table(rows: list[dict]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Create a display-friendly DataFrame from a list of row dictionaries."""
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

1. Load and audit the Palmer Penguins data¶

A computational-statistics workflow should start with the same discipline as any statistical analysis: understand the data-generating context, audit missingness, and identify which variables are suitable for each method.

We will mainly use:

  • bill_length_mm
  • bill_depth_mm
  • flipper_length_mm
  • body_mass_g
  • species

The species labels are available, but during the EM section we deliberately hide them and ask whether a Gaussian mixture can recover latent population structure.

In [3]:
@dataclass
class PenguinDataLoader:
    url: str = (
        'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/'
        'palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv'
    )
    cache_path: Path = Path('palmer_penguins.csv')

    def _offline_fallback(self) -> Optional[Path]:
        """Look for the same public dataset bundled by plotnine, if installed."""
        try:
            import plotnine
            candidate = Path(plotnine.__file__).resolve().parent / 'data' / 'penguins.csv'
            return candidate if candidate.exists() else None
        except Exception:
            return None

    def load(self) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        Prefer a local cache; otherwise download the official public CSV.
        If the machine is offline, use plotnine's bundled copy when available.
        """
        if self.cache_path.exists():
            df = pd.read_csv(self.cache_path)
            source = f'local cache: {self.cache_path}'
        else:
            try:
                df = pd.read_csv(self.url)
                df.to_csv(self.cache_path, index=False)
                source = self.url
            except Exception as exc:
                fallback = self._offline_fallback()
                if fallback is None:
                    raise RuntimeError(
                        'Could not download the Palmer Penguins CSV and no offline '
                        'plotnine copy was found. Connect to the internet once or place '
                        'penguins.csv beside this notebook as palmer_penguins.csv.'
                    ) from exc
                df = pd.read_csv(fallback)
                df.to_csv(self.cache_path, index=False)
                source = f'offline plotnine copy: {fallback}'
        print(f'Loaded {len(df):,} rows from {source}')
        return df

Missingness is modest, but several algorithms below require complete numeric vectors. Rather than inventing values by imputation and adding another modelling layer, we will use complete cases only for the variables needed by each experiment.

1.1 First visual question: do the species form visibly different populations?¶

This matters because several later methods—mixture simulation and EM in particular—implicitly assume that the observed population may be generated by multiple latent sub-populations.

What to notice¶

  • Gentoo penguins are visibly shifted toward longer flippers and larger body mass.
  • Adélie and Chinstrap overlap more strongly in this projection.
  • This is an ideal reminder that a latent-variable algorithm may find genuine structure without perfectly matching biological labels.
  • Later, EM will be evaluated both by likelihood (the model's own objective) and by agreement with species labels (an external diagnostic).

That distinction is important: clustering is not classification.

2. Random variate generation¶

Most pseudo-random generators fundamentally give us values that behave approximately like

[ U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1). ]

A central simulation problem is therefore:

[ U(0,1) \quad \longrightarrow \quad X \sim F. ]

We study four constructions:

  1. inverse transform sampling;
  2. rejection sampling;
  3. mixture / composition sampling;
  4. multivariate-normal generation via Cholesky factorisation.

2.1 Inverse-transform sampling¶

If (F) is a continuous CDF and (U\sim U(0,1)), then

[ X=F^{-1}(U) ]

has CDF (F).

For an exponential distribution with rate (\lambda),

[ F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x\ge 0, ]

so

[ X=-\frac{\log(1-U)}{\lambda}. ]

Because (1-U) is also uniform, (-\log U/\lambda) is equivalent.

We deliberately compare simulated moments with theoretical moments. This is a unit test for a stochastic algorithm.

In [8]:
def inverse_exponential(n: int, rate: float, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    if rate <= 0:
        raise ValueError('rate must be positive')
    u = rng.uniform(size=n)
    return -np.log1p(-u) / rate

rate = 2.0
x_exp = inverse_exponential(100_000, rate, rng)

inverse_check = pd.DataFrame({
    'quantity': ['mean', 'variance'],
    'theory': [1 / rate, 1 / rate**2],
    'simulation': [x_exp.mean(), x_exp.var(ddof=1)]
})
inverse_check['absolute_error'] = (inverse_check['simulation'] - inverse_check['theory']).abs()
inverse_check

p = figure(width=850, height=430, title='Inverse-transform sampling: simulated exponential density',
           x_axis_label='x', y_axis_label='density')
p.quad(top=hist, bottom=0, left=edges[:-1], right=edges[1:], alpha=0.35, legend_label='simulation')
p.line(xx, rate * np.exp(-rate * xx), line_width=3, legend_label='theoretical density')
p.legend.location = 'top_right'
show(p)

Interpretation¶

The empirical mean and variance should be close to

[ E[X]=1/\lambda, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2. ]

The important idea is not the exponential distribution itself. It is the transformation principle: a Uniform random variable becomes a draw from another distribution through a deterministic map.

Time complexity: (\Theta(n)).
Memory: (\Theta(n)) if all samples are retained; (\Theta(1)) is possible if moments are accumulated online.

2.2 Rejection sampling¶

Inverse transforms are inconvenient when (F^{-1}) is unavailable or expensive. Rejection sampling instead uses an easy proposal density (g(x)) and a constant (M) such that

[ f(x) \le M g(x). ]

Algorithm:

  1. draw (Y\sim g);
  2. draw (U\sim U(0,1));
  3. accept if

[ U \le \frac{f(Y)}{M g(Y)}. ]

We use a Beta(2,5) target on ([0,1]) and a Uniform proposal. This is deliberately simple enough that the correctness can be inspected visually.

In [10]:
@dataclass
class RejectionResult:
    samples: np.ndarray
    proposals: int
    acceptance_rate: float


def rejection_sample(
    target_pdf: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
    proposal_sampler: Callable[[int], np.ndarray],
    proposal_pdf: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
    M: float,
    n: int,
    rng: np.random.Generator,
    batch_size: int = 4096,
) -> RejectionResult:
    accepted = []
    proposals = 0

    while sum(map(len, accepted)) < n:
        y = proposal_sampler(batch_size)
        u = rng.uniform(size=batch_size)
        ratio = target_pdf(y) / (M * proposal_pdf(y))
        keep = y[u <= ratio]
        accepted.append(keep)
        proposals += batch_size

    samples = np.concatenate(accepted)[:n]
    return RejectionResult(samples, proposals, n / proposals)

beta_dist = stats.beta(a=2, b=5)
# With Uniform(0,1) proposal, M must exceed the maximum Beta density.
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 100_001)
M = beta_dist.pdf(grid).max() * 1.001

rej = rejection_sample(
    target_pdf=beta_dist.pdf,
    proposal_sampler=lambda m: rng.uniform(0, 1, size=m),
    proposal_pdf=lambda y: np.ones_like(y),
    M=M,
    n=50_000,
    rng=rng,
)

pd.DataFrame({
    'M': [M],
    'theoretical_acceptance_approx': [1/M],
    'observed_acceptance_rate': [rej.acceptance_rate],
    'accepted_samples': [len(rej.samples)],
    'proposal_draws': [rej.proposals],
})

           x_axis_label='x', y_axis_label='density')
p.quad(top=hist, bottom=0, left=edges[:-1], right=edges[1:], alpha=0.35, legend_label='accepted samples')
p.line(xx, beta_dist.pdf(xx), line_width=3, legend_label='target Beta(2,5)')
p.line(xx, np.full_like(xx, M), line_dash='dashed', line_width=2, legend_label='M × Uniform envelope')
p.legend.location = 'top_right'
show(p)

Tuning lesson: envelope quality matters¶

For normalized (f) and (g), the idealized acceptance probability is approximately (1/M). A loose envelope means wasted proposals.

A rejection sampler can therefore be mathematically correct but computationally poor.

This distinction—correctness versus efficiency—will recur in importance sampling and MCMC.

2.3 Composition sampling from an empirical species mixture¶

The penguin population naturally suggests a finite mixture. Let

[ Z\in{\text{Adelie},\text{Chinstrap},\text{Gentoo}} ]

identify the species component. If

[ P(Z=k)=\pi_k ]

and body mass within component (k) is approximated by a Gaussian,

[ X\mid Z=k \sim N(\mu_k,\sigma_k^2), ]

then we can simulate from the mixture by:

  1. sampling the component (Z);
  2. sampling (X\mid Z).

This is the forward-data-generating view of a mixture model. EM later tackles the inverse problem: given X but not Z, infer the mixture parameters and latent memberships.

In [12]:
body_by_species = (
    penguins.groupby('species')['body_mass_g']
    .agg(['count', 'mean', 'std'])
    .reset_index()
)
body_by_species['weight'] = body_by_species['count'] / body_by_species['count'].sum()
body_by_species

def simulate_species_mixture(n: int, summary: pd.DataFrame, rng: np.random.Generator) -> pd.DataFrame:
    labels = summary['species'].to_numpy()
    weights = summary['weight'].to_numpy()
    means = dict(zip(summary['species'], summary['mean']))
    sds = dict(zip(summary['species'], summary['std']))

    z = rng.choice(labels, size=n, p=weights)
    x = np.array([rng.normal(means[k], sds[k]) for k in z])
    return pd.DataFrame({'species_component': z, 'simulated_body_mass_g': x})

mix_sim = simulate_species_mixture(50_000, body_by_species, rng)

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'quantity': ['mean body mass', 'SD body mass'],
    'observed_data': [penguins['body_mass_g'].mean(), penguins['body_mass_g'].std(ddof=1)],
    'mixture_simulation': [mix_sim['simulated_body_mass_g'].mean(), mix_sim['simulated_body_mass_g'].std(ddof=1)]
})
comparison
Out[13]:
quantity observed_data mixture_simulation
0 mean body mass 4,201.7544 4,197.4107
1 SD body mass 801.9545 804.9396

Interpretation¶

If the Gaussian-within-species approximation is reasonable, the simulated mixture should reproduce broad distributional features such as the overall mean and spread. It will not reproduce every empirical detail because we have deliberately compressed each species into only three numbers: (\pi_k,\mu_k,\sigma_k).

This distinction is essential:

Simulation reproduces the assumptions of a model—not necessarily every feature of reality.

2.4 Multivariate normal generation with Cholesky factorisation¶

For a multivariate normal target

[ X\sim N_d(\mu,\Sigma), ]

factor the covariance matrix as

[ \Sigma = LL^\top. ]

If (Z\sim N(0,I)), then

[ X = \mu + LZ ]

has the desired mean and covariance.

We estimate (\mu) and (\Sigma) from the two-dimensional Gentoo variables

[ (\text{flipper length},\text{body mass}). ]

In [14]:
gentoo2 = penguins.loc[penguins['species'] == 'Gentoo', ['flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g']].dropna()
mu = gentoo2.mean().to_numpy()
Sigma = gentoo2.cov().to_numpy()
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)

z = rng.normal(size=(50_000, 2))
sim_mv = mu + z @ L.T

mv_validation = pd.DataFrame({
    'quantity': ['mean flipper', 'mean mass', 'var flipper', 'var mass', 'covariance'],
    'target': [mu[0], mu[1], Sigma[0,0], Sigma[1,1], Sigma[0,1]],
    'simulation': [
        sim_mv[:,0].mean(), sim_mv[:,1].mean(),
        sim_mv[:,0].var(ddof=1), sim_mv[:,1].var(ddof=1),
        np.cov(sim_mv.T, ddof=1)[0,1]
    ]
})
mv_validation['relative_error'] = (
    (mv_validation['simulation'] - mv_validation['target']) /
    mv_validation['target'].replace(0, np.nan)
).abs()
mv_validation

Complexity¶

For a dense (d\times d) covariance matrix:

  • Cholesky factorisation: (\Theta(d^3)) once;
  • each new multivariate draw: (\Theta(d^2));
  • (n) draws after factorisation: (\Theta(nd^2)).

That distinction matters when a covariance is reused for millions of draws: the one-time factorisation cost can be amortized.

3. Monte Carlo estimation: integration becomes averaging¶

Suppose the quantity of interest is

[ I = E_f[h(X)] = \int h(x)f(x),dx. ]

If (X_1,\ldots,X_n\overset{iid}{\sim}f), then

[ \hat I_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i) ]

converges to (I) by the law of large numbers.

The central-limit theorem gives the characteristic Monte Carlo error rate

[ SE(\hat I_n) \approx \frac{\sigma_h}{\sqrt n}. ]

This is powerful but slow: reducing Monte Carlo error by a factor of 10 generally requires roughly 100 times more samples.

Case-study question¶

Using our fitted species mixture for body mass, estimate

[ P(X > 5000\text{ g}). ]

Because the fitted components are Gaussian, an analytic answer is available. We use that answer only as a benchmark for Monte Carlo convergence.

In [15]:
def mixture_tail_probability(threshold: float, summary: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    return float(np.sum(
        summary['weight'].to_numpy() *
        stats.norm.sf(
            threshold,
            loc=summary['mean'].to_numpy(),
            scale=summary['std'].to_numpy()
        )
    ))

threshold = 5000.0
truth_tail = mixture_tail_probability(threshold, body_by_species)

mc_draws = simulate_species_mixture(200_000, body_by_species, rng)['simulated_body_mass_g'].to_numpy()
ind = (mc_draws > threshold).astype(float)
running = np.cumsum(ind) / np.arange(1, len(ind) + 1)

mc_est = ind.mean()
mc_se = ind.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(ind))

pd.DataFrame({
    'target': ['P(body mass > 5000g)'],
    'analytic_under_fitted_mixture': [truth_tail],
    'monte_carlo_estimate': [mc_est],
    'monte_carlo_SE': [mc_se],
    'absolute_error': [abs(mc_est - truth_tail)]
})
Out[15]:
target analytic_under_fitted_mixture monte_carlo_estimate monte_carlo_SE absolute_error

In [16]:
idx = np.unique(np.geomspace(10, len(running), 700).astype(int)) - 1
p = figure(width=900, height=440,
           title='Monte Carlo convergence of tail-probability estimate',
           x_axis_type='log', x_axis_label='number of simulated draws (log scale)',
           y_axis_label='running estimate')
p.line(idx + 1, running[idx], line_width=2, legend_label='running Monte Carlo estimate')
p.add_layout(Span(location=truth_tail, dimension='width', line_dash='dashed', line_width=2))
p.legend.location = 'top_right'
show(p)

Interpretation¶

The running estimate fluctuates heavily at small (n), then stabilizes. The fluctuation scale contracts approximately as (n^{-1/2}).

This motivates the next question:

Can we reduce variance without simply increasing n?

4. Variance reduction¶

A variance-reduction method tries to construct another estimator with the same target but smaller variance.

We study:

  1. antithetic variates — introduce useful negative dependence;
  2. control variates — exploit a correlated quantity with known expectation;
  3. importance sampling — spend simulation effort in the region that matters most.

4.1 Antithetic variates¶

If (Z\sim N(0,1)), then (-Z\sim N(0,1)). For a monotone nonlinear function, evaluating both can induce negative covariance.

To make validation exact, estimate

[ E[e^Z] = e^{1/2}. ]

Ordinary Monte Carlo uses independent (Z_i). Antithetic Monte Carlo uses pairs ((Z_i,-Z_i)):

[ \hat I_A = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{e^{Z_i}+e^{-Z_i}}{2}. ]

In [17]:
def antithetic_experiment(n_pairs: int, repetitions: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> pd.DataFrame:
    ordinary = np.empty(repetitions)
    anti = np.empty(repetitions)

    for r in range(repetitions):
        # Same total number of function evaluations: 2*n_pairs.
        z_ord = rng.normal(size=2*n_pairs)
        ordinary[r] = np.exp(z_ord).mean()

        z = rng.normal(size=n_pairs)
        anti[r] = ((np.exp(z) + np.exp(-z)) / 2).mean()

    return pd.DataFrame({'ordinary': ordinary, 'antithetic': anti})

anti_exp = antithetic_experiment(n_pairs=1_000, repetitions=600, rng=rng)
truth = np.exp(0.5)

anti_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'method': ['ordinary MC', 'antithetic'],
    'mean_estimate': [anti_exp['ordinary'].mean(), anti_exp['antithetic'].mean()],
    'empirical_variance_across_runs': [anti_exp['ordinary'].var(ddof=1), anti_exp['antithetic'].var(ddof=1)]
})
anti_summary['variance_ratio_vs_ordinary'] = (
    anti_summary['empirical_variance_across_runs'] /
    anti_summary.loc[0, 'empirical_variance_across_runs']
)
anti_summary['truth'] = truth
anti_summary
Out[17]:
method mean_estimate empirical_variance_across_runs variance_ratio_vs_ordinary truth
0 ordinary MC 1.6486 0.0022 1.0000 1.6487
1 antithetic 1.6476 0.0015 0.6714 1.6487

Reading the table¶

The means should both be close to (e^{1/2}), so both estimators target the same expectation. The meaningful comparison is the variance across repeated experiments.

If the antithetic variance ratio is below 1, we obtained more precision from essentially the same number of function evaluations.

4.2 Control variates using Gentoo body mass¶

Suppose a fitted model tells us that

[ X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2) ]

for Gentoo body mass, and we want

[ E[X^2]. ]

The exact target is

[ E[X^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2. ]

Pretend this second moment is hard to calculate but (E[X]=\mu) is known. Then (X) is a natural control variate for (X^2).

Construct

[ \hat\theta_c = \bar Y - c(\bar X-\mu), \qquad Y=X^2. ]

The variance-minimizing coefficient is

[ c^*=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Y,X)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)}. ]

In [18]:
gentoo_mass = penguins.loc[penguins['species'] == 'Gentoo', 'body_mass_g'].to_numpy()
mu_g = gentoo_mass.mean()
sd_g = gentoo_mass.std(ddof=1)
truth_second_moment = mu_g**2 + sd_g**2


def control_variate_once(n: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    x = rng.normal(mu_g, sd_g, size=n)
    y = x**2
    naive = y.mean()
    c_hat = np.cov(y, x, ddof=1)[0, 1] / np.var(x, ddof=1)
    controlled = y.mean() - c_hat * (x.mean() - mu_g)
    return naive, controlled, c_hat

rows = [control_variate_once(2_000, rng) for _ in range(500)]
cv_runs = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['naive', 'control_variate', 'c_hat'])

cv_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'method': ['naive MC', 'control variate'],
    'mean_estimate': [cv_runs['naive'].mean(), cv_runs['control_variate'].mean()],
    'variance_across_runs': [cv_runs['naive'].var(ddof=1), cv_runs['control_variate'].var(ddof=1)]
})
cv_summary['variance_reduction_percent'] = (
    1 - cv_summary['variance_across_runs'] / cv_summary.loc[0, 'variance_across_runs']
) * 100
cv_summary['target_E_X2'] = truth_second_moment
cv_summary

method mean_estimate variance_across_runs variance_reduction_percent target_E_X2
0 naive MC 26,018,269.7027 11,528,204,996.9626 0.0000 26,020,074.2535
1 control variate 26,020,106.3506 66,184,261.1145 99.4259 26,020,074.2535

Why this works¶

The raw estimator (\bar Y) fluctuates partly because the simulated sample happens to contain too many heavy or light penguins. The control term detects that imbalance through (\bar X-\mu) and corrects for it.

This reveals a deep connection:

A control variate is essentially a regression adjustment inside a Monte Carlo estimator.

4.3 Importance sampling for a rare Gentoo body-mass tail¶

Rare-event estimation is a canonical Monte Carlo failure mode. Suppose the fitted Gentoo model is

[ X\sim N(\mu_G,\sigma_G^2) ]

and we want

[ p=P(X>6500\text{ g}). ]

Naive simulation wastes almost all draws far below 6500 g.

Importance sampling changes the proposal from (f) to a strategically shifted (g):

[ p = E_g\left[I(X>6500)\frac{f(X)}{g(X)}\right]. ]

The ratio

[ w(X)=\frac{f(X)}{g(X)} ]

corrects the deliberate sampling distortion.

In [19]:
rare_threshold = 6500.0
f = stats.norm(loc=mu_g, scale=sd_g)
true_rare = f.sf(rare_threshold)


def naive_tail(n: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> float:
    x = rng.normal(mu_g, sd_g, size=n)
    return np.mean(x > rare_threshold)


def importance_tail(n: int, proposal_mu: float, proposal_sd: float, rng: np.random.Generator):
    g = stats.norm(loc=proposal_mu, scale=proposal_sd)
    x = g.rvs(size=n, random_state=rng)
    logw = f.logpdf(x) - g.logpdf(x)
    contribution = (x > rare_threshold) * np.exp(logw)
    estimate = contribution.mean()

    # Weight ESS is a diagnostic; here it describes weight concentration.
    w = np.exp(logw - np.max(logw))
    ess = (w.sum() ** 2) / np.sum(w**2)
    return estimate, ess, np.max(logw), np.quantile(logw, 0.99)

R = 400
n_each = 4_000
is_good_mu = rare_threshold + 0.25 * sd_g
is_good_sd = sd_g
is_bad_mu = mu_g - 2 * sd_g
is_bad_sd = 0.55 * sd_g

naive_vals = []
good_vals = []
bad_vals = []
good_diag = []
bad_diag = []

for _ in range(R):
    naive_vals.append(naive_tail(n_each, rng))
    e, ess, mx, q99 = importance_tail(n_each, is_good_mu, is_good_sd, rng)
    good_vals.append(e); good_diag.append((ess, mx, q99))
    e, ess, mx, q99 = importance_tail(n_each, is_bad_mu, is_bad_sd, rng)
    bad_vals.append(e); bad_diag.append((ess, mx, q99))

methods = ['naive MC', 'good importance proposal', 'bad importance proposal']

The important lesson is not “importance sampling is always better”¶

A good proposal deliberately places samples where the integrand (I(X>6500)f(X)) matters. A poor proposal can create huge, unstable importance weights.

Diagnostics to watch:

  • estimator variance over repeated runs;
  • maximum / upper-tail log weights;
  • effective sample size of normalized weights;
  • whether a few observations dominate the estimate.

Failure mode: a proposal can have the correct mathematical support and still have terrible variance because its tails are badly matched to the target.

5. Expectation–Maximization (EM): learning hidden population structure¶

Now we reverse the mixture-simulation problem.

We observe morphology (X_i) but pretend the species labels (Z_i) are hidden. Assume a K-component Gaussian mixture:

[ p(x_i)=\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k,N(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k). ]

The observed-data log-likelihood is

[ \ell(\theta)=\sum_i \log\left(\sum_k \pi_k f_k(x_i)\right), ]

which contains a difficult log(sum(...)) structure.

If component labels were known, estimation would be easy. EM alternates:

E-step¶

Compute posterior responsibilities

[ \gamma_{ik}=P(Z_i=k\mid X_i,\theta^{(t)}). ]

M-step¶

Treat (\gamma_{ik}) as fractional membership weights and update

[ \pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k. ]

We implement a 2-dimensional, 3-component Gaussian mixture from scratch using bill length and flipper length.

In [22]:
@dataclass
class EMResult:
    weights: np.ndarray
    means: np.ndarray
    covariances: np.ndarray
    responsibilities: np.ndarray
    log_likelihood_history: list[float]
    converged: bool
    iterations: int


class GaussianMixtureEM:
    def __init__(self, n_components: int, max_iter: int = 300, tol: float = 1e-6,
                 reg_covar: float = 1e-5, random_state: int = 0):
        self.K = n_components
        self.max_iter = max_iter
        self.tol = tol
        self.reg_covar = reg_covar
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)

    @staticmethod
    def _log_gaussian(X, mean, cov):
        d = X.shape[1]
        cov = cov + 1e-12 * np.eye(d)
        sign, logdet = np.linalg.slogdet(cov)
        if sign <= 0:
            raise np.linalg.LinAlgError('Covariance is not positive definite.')
        diff = X - mean
        sol = np.linalg.solve(cov, diff.T).T
        quad = np.sum(diff * sol, axis=1)
        return -0.5 * (d * np.log(2*np.pi) + logdet + quad)

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray) -> EMResult:
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        n, d = X.shape

        # Random-observation initialization deliberately exposes local-optimum sensitivity.
        init_idx = self.rng.choice(n, size=self.K, replace=False)
        means = X[init_idx].copy()
        base_cov = np.cov(X.T) + self.reg_covar * np.eye(d)
        covs = np.stack([base_cov.copy() for _ in range(self.K)])
        weights = np.full(self.K, 1/self.K)

        ll_history = []
        converged = False

        for iteration in range(1, self.max_iter + 1):
            # E-step in log space for stability.
            log_joint = np.column_stack([
                np.log(weights[k] + 1e-300) + self._log_gaussian(X, means[k], covs[k])
                for k in range(self.K)
            ])
            log_norm = logsumexp(log_joint, axis=1)
            resp = np.exp(log_joint - log_norm[:, None])
            ll = float(log_norm.sum())
            ll_history.append(ll)

            # M-step.
            Nk = resp.sum(axis=0) + 1e-12
            weights = Nk / n
            means = (resp.T @ X) / Nk[:, None]

            new_covs = np.empty((self.K, d, d))
            for k in range(self.K):
                diff = X - means[k]
                weighted = diff * resp[:, [k]]
                cov = (weighted.T @ diff) / Nk[k]
                cov += self.reg_covar * np.eye(d)
                new_covs[k] = cov
            covs = new_covs

            if iteration > 1:
                improvement = ll_history[-1] - ll_history[-2]
                if abs(improvement) <= self.tol * (1 + abs(ll_history[-2])):
                    converged = True
                    break

        return EMResult(weights, means, covs, resp, ll_history, converged, iteration)

5.1 Scale the features before EM¶

Gaussian likelihoods are sensitive to scale. Body mass measured in thousands of grams would dominate bill length measured in tens of millimetres if used raw.

For this experiment we use bill length and flipper length, but still standardize them:

[ Z_j=\frac{X_j-\bar X_j}{s_j}. ]

The transformation does not create cluster separation; it only puts the axes on comparable numerical scales.

In [23]:
features = ['bill_length_mm', 'flipper_length_mm']
X_df = penguins[features].copy()
X_mean = X_df.mean().to_numpy()
X_sd = X_df.std(ddof=1).to_numpy()
X = (X_df.to_numpy() - X_mean) / X_sd
true_species = penguins['species'].to_numpy()

# Multiple starts: EM can converge to different local maxima.
results = []
for seed in range(12):
    model = GaussianMixtureEM(3, random_state=seed, reg_covar=1e-4)
    res = model.fit(X)
    pred = res.responsibilities.argmax(axis=1)
    ari = adjusted_rand_score(true_species, pred)
    results.append((seed, res, ari))

runs_table = pd.DataFrame({
    'seed': [s for s,_,_ in results],
    'final_log_likelihood': [r.log_likelihood_history[-1] for _,r,_ in results],
    'iterations': [r.iterations for _,r,_ in results],
    'converged': [r.converged for _,r,_ in results],
    'ARI_vs_species': [ari for _,_,ari in results],
}).sort_values('final_log_likelihood', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

How to read this multi-start table¶

  • Final log-likelihood is EM's own objective. Higher is better under the assumed mixture model.
  • ARI (Adjusted Rand Index) compares discovered clusters with species labels. It is external information and is not optimized by EM.
  • Different seeds may converge to different likelihoods, demonstrating local-optimum sensitivity.

A robust workflow normally runs EM from multiple initializations and keeps the highest-likelihood solution—not the one that best matches labels that would be unavailable in a genuine unsupervised problem.

EM interpretation and failure modes¶

  1. Responsibilities are soft assignments. An observation can be 60% component 1 and 40% component 2.
  2. Likelihood should not decrease apart from tiny floating-point error.
  3. EM is not globally optimal. Multiple starts are a practical requirement.
  4. Gaussian components are assumptions. Biological species need not have exactly elliptical Gaussian morphology.
  5. Covariance collapse is possible. If one component captures too few points, its covariance can become nearly singular; reg_covar protects numerical stability.
  6. Cluster labels are arbitrary. Component 0 has no intrinsic meaning until interpreted.

Per iteration with full covariances, the dominant cost is roughly (\Theta(nKd^2)) plus covariance linear algebra. For small (d), this is usually very manageable.

6. Markov chains: the machinery underneath MCMC¶

A sequence (X_0,X_1,\ldots) is Markov if

[ P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\ldots)=P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t). ]

For a finite-state chain with transition matrix (P), a stationary distribution (\pi) satisfies

[ \pi P = \pi. ]

MCMC exploits this idea in reverse: rather than merely analysing a given Markov chain, we design a chain whose stationary distribution is the distribution we want to sample from.

Before continuous-state MCMC, we verify the stationary-distribution idea using a small three-state chain.

In [28]:
P = np.array([
    [0.80, 0.15, 0.05],
    [0.20, 0.60, 0.20],
    [0.05, 0.20, 0.75],
])

# Solve pi P = pi using the eigenvector associated with eigenvalue 1.
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eig(P.T)
idx1 = np.argmin(np.abs(eigvals - 1))
pi = np.real(eigvecs[:, idx1])
pi = pi / pi.sum()

states = ['A', 'B', 'C']
stationary_table = pd.DataFrame({'state': states, 'stationary_probability': pi})

Key intuition¶

The chain gradually “forgets” its starting state and approaches the same long-run distribution. MCMC asks us to engineer this phenomenon for a complicated target density.

7. Metropolis–Hastings MCMC¶

Bayesian case-study question¶

For Gentoo body mass, estimate the posterior distribution of the population mean (\mu).

To make validation possible, assume:

[ X_i\mid\mu \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), ]

with (\sigma) fixed at the empirical Gentoo standard deviation and prior

[ \mu\sim N(m_0,s_0^2). ]

This model is conjugate, so we know the exact posterior. But we will intentionally use Metropolis–Hastings as if the posterior were not available in closed form.

That gives us a gold-standard test of the MCMC implementation.

In [30]:
@dataclass
class MHResult:
    chain: np.ndarray
    accepted: np.ndarray
    acceptance_rate: float


class RandomWalkMetropolis:
    def __init__(self, log_target: Callable[[float], float], proposal_sd: float,
                 rng: np.random.Generator):
        self.log_target = log_target
        self.proposal_sd = proposal_sd
        self.rng = rng

    def sample(self, initial: float, n_iter: int) -> MHResult:
        chain = np.empty(n_iter)
        accepted = np.zeros(n_iter, dtype=bool)
        x = float(initial)
        logp_x = self.log_target(x)

        for t in range(n_iter):
            y = x + self.rng.normal(scale=self.proposal_sd)
            logp_y = self.log_target(y)
            log_alpha = min(0.0, logp_y - logp_x)  # symmetric proposal
            if np.log(self.rng.uniform()) < log_alpha:
                x = y
                logp_x = logp_y
                accepted[t] = True
            chain[t] = x

        return MHResult(chain, accepted, accepted.mean())
In [31]:
y = gentoo_mass
n = len(y)
sigma_known = sd_g
m0 = 4800.0
s0 = 800.0


def log_posterior_mu(mu: float) -> float:
    log_prior = stats.norm.logpdf(mu, loc=m0, scale=s0)
    log_lik = np.sum(stats.norm.logpdf(y, loc=mu, scale=sigma_known))
    return float(log_prior + log_lik)

# Exact conjugate posterior for validation.
post_var = 1 / (1/s0**2 + n/sigma_known**2)
post_mean = post_var * (m0/s0**2 + n*y.mean()/sigma_known**2)
post_sd = np.sqrt(post_var)

proposal_sd = 80.0
mh = RandomWalkMetropolis(log_posterior_mu, proposal_sd, rng)
mh_res = mh.sample(initial=y.mean() - 500, n_iter=20_000)
burn = 3_000
mh_post = mh_res.chain[burn:]

pd.DataFrame({
    'quantity': ['posterior mean', 'posterior SD'],
    'analytic': [post_mean, post_sd],
    'MCMC': [mh_post.mean(), mh_post.std(ddof=1)]
}).assign(acceptance_rate=mh_res.acceptance_rate)

7.1 MCMC diagnostics: trace, autocorrelation, and ESS¶

MCMC draws are not IID. Consecutive states can be highly correlated, so 10,000 iterations may contain far less information than 10,000 independent draws.

For autocorrelation (\rho_k), an approximate effective sample size is

[ ESS \approx \frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k}. ]

We use the initial-positive-sequence idea: sum positive paired autocorrelations until the sequence turns non-positive. This is more stable than blindly summing noisy high-lag correlations.

In [32]:
def autocorrelation(x: np.ndarray, max_lag: int = 200) -> np.ndarray:
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    x = x - x.mean()
    denom = np.dot(x, x)
    acf = np.empty(max_lag + 1)
    acf[0] = 1.0
    for lag in range(1, max_lag + 1):
        acf[lag] = np.dot(x[:-lag], x[lag:]) / denom
    return acf


def effective_sample_size(x: np.ndarray, max_lag: int = 1000) -> float:
    acf = autocorrelation(x, min(max_lag, len(x)//4))
    total = 0.0
    # Geyer's paired initial-positive sequence (simplified).
    k = 1
    while k + 1 < len(acf):
        pair = acf[k] + acf[k+1]
        if pair <= 0:
            break
        total += pair
        k += 2
    return len(x) / (1 + 2*total)

mh_acf = autocorrelation(mh_post, 80)
mh_ess = effective_sample_size(mh_post)

pd.DataFrame({
    'iterations_after_burn_in': [len(mh_post)],
    'acceptance_rate': [mh_res.acceptance_rate],
    'ESS': [mh_ess],
    'ESS_fraction': [mh_ess/len(mh_post)],
    'posterior_mean_error_vs_exact': [mh_post.mean()-post_mean]
})

7.2 Proposal-scale tuning experiment¶

A random-walk proposal

[ Y = X_t + \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon\sim N(0,s_q^2) ]

has a classic trade-off:

  • very small (s_q): high acceptance but tiny movements → strong autocorrelation;
  • very large (s_q): large proposed movements but many rejections;
  • useful intermediate scale: better exploration per iteration.

Acceptance rate alone is not the objective. ESS per iteration is closer to what we actually care about.

In [34]:
tuning_rows = []
for psd in [5, 20, 50, 80, 150, 300, 700]:
    local_rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_SEED + int(psd))
    res = RandomWalkMetropolis(log_posterior_mu, psd, local_rng).sample(y.mean(), 12_000)
    c = res.chain[2_000:]
    ess = effective_sample_size(c)
    tuning_rows.append({
        'proposal_sd': psd,
        'acceptance_rate': res.acceptance_rate,
        'ESS': ess,
        'ESS_per_1000_iterations': ess/len(c)*1000,
        'posterior_mean': c.mean(),
        'abs_error_vs_exact': abs(c.mean()-post_mean)
    })

mh_tuning = pd.DataFrame(tuning_rows)

MCMC failure checklist¶

A chain can return numbers without being useful. Before trusting it, ask:

  • Did multiple initializations reach the same region?
  • Is the trace mixing or slowly drifting?
  • Is autocorrelation excessive?
  • Is ESS large enough for the desired precision?
  • Does proposal tuning materially improve ESS?
  • Are posterior conclusions stable after changing burn-in or chain length?

The deepest MCMC principle is:

The number of stored iterations is not the amount of independent information.

8. Gibbs sampling: Bayesian mean and variance jointly¶

Metropolis–Hastings proposes a candidate and may reject it. Gibbs sampling can be simpler when the full conditional distributions are available.

For a Normal likelihood with unknown mean and variance, use the conjugate Normal–Inverse-Gamma structure:

[ X_i\mid\mu,\sigma^2 \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), ]

[ \mu\mid\sigma^2 \sim N(m_0,\sigma^2/\kappa_0), ]

[ \sigma^2\sim \mathrm{InvGamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0). ]

Then the full conditionals are known, so we alternate draws from

[ \mu\mid\sigma^2,X ]

and

[ \sigma^2\mid\mu,X. ]

This is a two-block Gibbs sampler.

In [36]:
@dataclass
class GibbsResult:
    mu: np.ndarray
    sigma2: np.ndarray


def gibbs_normal_unknown_variance(
    y: np.ndarray,
    n_iter: int,
    m0: float,
    kappa0: float,
    alpha0: float,
    beta0: float,
    rng: np.random.Generator,
) -> GibbsResult:
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    n = len(y)
    mu_chain = np.empty(n_iter)
    sigma2_chain = np.empty(n_iter)

    mu = y.mean()
    sigma2 = y.var(ddof=1)

    for t in range(n_iter):
        # mu | sigma2, y
        kappa_n = kappa0 + n
        m_n = (kappa0*m0 + n*y.mean()) / kappa_n
        mu = rng.normal(m_n, np.sqrt(sigma2/kappa_n))

        # sigma2 | mu, y
        alpha_n = alpha0 + (n + 1)/2
        beta_n = beta0 + 0.5*np.sum((y-mu)**2) + 0.5*kappa0*(mu-m0)**2
        sigma2 = stats.invgamma.rvs(a=alpha_n, scale=beta_n, random_state=rng)

        mu_chain[t] = mu
        sigma2_chain[t] = sigma2

    return GibbsResult(mu_chain, sigma2_chain)


gibbs = gibbs_normal_unknown_variance(
    y=gentoo_mass,
    n_iter=20_000,
    m0=4800,
    kappa0=0.1,
    alpha0=2.0,
    beta0=200_000,
    rng=np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_SEED + 99),
)

g_burn = 3_000
g_mu = gibbs.mu[g_burn:]
g_sd = np.sqrt(gibbs.sigma2[g_burn:])

pd.DataFrame({
    'parameter': ['mu', 'sigma'],
    'posterior_mean': [g_mu.mean(), g_sd.mean()],
    'posterior_2.5%': [np.quantile(g_mu,.025), np.quantile(g_sd,.025)],
    'posterior_97.5%': [np.quantile(g_mu,.975), np.quantile(g_sd,.975)],
    'empirical_data_estimate': [gentoo_mass.mean(), gentoo_mass.std(ddof=1)],
    'ESS': [effective_sample_size(g_mu), effective_sample_size(g_sd)]
})

Gibbs versus Metropolis–Hastings¶

Feature Metropolis–Hastings Gibbs
Proposal design Required Not in the usual accept/reject sense
Rejections Possible Every full-conditional draw is accepted
Requirement Target ratio evaluable Full conditionals must be sampleable
Tuning Often important Usually less proposal tuning
Correlation Can be high Can still be high when parameters are strongly coupled

Gibbs is not “independent sampling.” It still produces a Markov chain, so autocorrelation and ESS remain important.

9. Bootstrap: simulate the sampling distribution from the empirical distribution¶

Suppose the estimator is

[ \hat\theta=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n) ]

and its analytic sampling distribution is inconvenient.

The nonparametric bootstrap replaces the unknown population distribution (F) by the empirical distribution (F_n), then repeatedly resamples observations with replacement.

Case-study estimand¶

Estimate the difference in median body mass:

[ \Delta = \mathrm{median}(X_G)-\mathrm{median}(X_A), ]

where (G) denotes Gentoo and (A) denotes Adélie.

The median is deliberately chosen because its finite-sample variance is less convenient than the mean's.

In [38]:
adelie_mass = penguins.loc[penguins['species']=='Adelie', 'body_mass_g'].to_numpy()

def median_difference(g: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.median(g) - np.median(a))

observed_delta = median_difference(gentoo_mass, adelie_mass)


def bootstrap_two_sample_stat(
    x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, stat: Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray], float],
    B: int, rng: np.random.Generator
) -> np.ndarray:
    out = np.empty(B)
    nx, ny = len(x), len(y)
    for b in range(B):
        xb = x[rng.integers(0, nx, size=nx)]
        yb = y[rng.integers(0, ny, size=ny)]
        out[b] = stat(xb, yb)
    return out

boot = bootstrap_two_sample_stat(
    gentoo_mass, adelie_mass, median_difference,
    B=8_000, rng=np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_SEED + 7)
)

boot_se = boot.std(ddof=1)
boot_bias = boot.mean() - observed_delta
ci_pct = np.quantile(boot, [0.025, 0.975])

bootstrap_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'observed_median_difference_g': [observed_delta],
    'bootstrap_mean': [boot.mean()],
    'bootstrap_bias_estimate': [boot_bias],
    'bootstrap_SE': [boot_se],
    'percentile_CI_2.5%': [ci_pct[0]],
    'percentile_CI_97.5%': [ci_pct[1]],
    'bootstrap_replicates': [len(boot)]
})
bootstrap_summary

           x_axis_label='bootstrap median difference (g)', y_axis_label='density')

Interpretation¶

The bootstrap distribution approximates the repeated-sampling distribution of the estimator under the empirical distribution.

From it we can estimate:

  • standard error: spread of bootstrap replicates;
  • bias: bootstrap mean minus the original estimate;
  • confidence interval: here, the 2.5% and 97.5% bootstrap quantiles.

What the bootstrap does not fix¶

  • biased or unrepresentative original sampling;
  • dependence that is ignored by IID resampling;
  • tiny samples with little information;
  • inappropriate resampling units.

For time series, spatial data, clusters, or repeated measurements, the resampling scheme must respect dependence.

Complexity: if statistic computation costs (C(n)), then (B) replicates cost approximately (\Theta(B C(n))).

9.1 How many bootstrap replicates are enough?¶

There are two sources of uncertainty:

  1. the statistical uncertainty in the original dataset;
  2. the Monte Carlo uncertainty from using only a finite number (B) of bootstrap replicates.

Increasing (B) reduces only the second.

In [40]:
B_grid = [200, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000]
boot_convergence = []
for B in B_grid:
    b = boot[:B]
    q = np.quantile(b, [0.025, .975])
    boot_convergence.append({
        'B': B,
        'SE': b.std(ddof=1),
        'bias': b.mean() - observed_delta,
        'CI_low': q[0],
        'CI_high': q[1]
    })

Practical reading¶

If the estimated SE and confidence limits are still moving noticeably as (B) increases, the bootstrap simulation itself is too noisy. If they have stabilized, further increases in (B) may add computation with little practical benefit.

10. Jackknife: deterministic leave-one-out resampling¶

The jackknife creates (n) leave-one-out estimates

[ \hat\theta_{(-i)}=T(X_1,\ldots,X_{i-1},X_{i+1},\ldots,X_n). ]

For a one-sample statistic, a common variance estimate is

[ \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}{jack} =\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_i(\hat\theta{(-i)}-\bar\theta_{(-)})^2. ]

To make the comparison clean, consider the Gentoo mean body mass. For a smooth statistic like the mean, jackknife and familiar analytic formulas should agree closely.

In [41]:
def jackknife_one_sample(x: np.ndarray, stat: Callable[[np.ndarray], float]):
    n = len(x)
    vals = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        vals[i] = stat(np.delete(x, i))
    avg = vals.mean()
    var = (n-1)/n * np.sum((vals-avg)**2)
    se = np.sqrt(var)
    bias = (n-1) * (avg - stat(x))
    return vals, se, bias

jack_vals, jack_se, jack_bias = jackknife_one_sample(gentoo_mass, np.mean)
analytic_se = gentoo_mass.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(gentoo_mass))

# Bootstrap same statistic for comparison.
boot_mean = np.empty(5000)
local_rng = np.random.default_rng(RANDOM_SEED + 101)
for b in range(len(boot_mean)):
    xb = gentoo_mass[local_rng.integers(0, len(gentoo_mass), size=len(gentoo_mass))]
    boot_mean[b] = xb.mean()

pd.DataFrame({
    'method': ['analytic mean formula', 'jackknife', 'bootstrap'],
    'SE_estimate': [analytic_se, jack_se, boot_mean.std(ddof=1)],
    'bias_estimate': [np.nan, jack_bias, boot_mean.mean()-gentoo_mass.mean()]
})

Jackknife versus bootstrap¶

Question Jackknife Bootstrap
Resampling Delete one observation systematically Sample with replacement
Number of replicates Usually (n) User-chosen (B), often thousands
Randomness conditional on data None Yes
Cost Often lower Often higher
Smooth statistics Very effective Effective
Non-smooth statistics such as extreme quantiles Can behave poorly Usually more flexible

A useful mental model is that the jackknife approximates how the estimator changes under a small local perturbation of the empirical distribution, whereas the bootstrap more fully simulates repeated empirical samples.

11. Advanced extension — empirical likelihood for a mean¶

Empirical likelihood combines a likelihood-style ratio with nonparametric probability weights.

Given observations (x_1,\ldots,x_n), assign probabilities (p_i) to the observed support points and maximize

[ L=\prod_{i=1}^n p_i ]

subject to

[ p_i\ge0,\qquad \sum_i p_i=1, ]

and, for a hypothesized mean (\mu),

[ \sum_i p_i(x_i-\mu)=0. ]

The solution has the form

[ p_i=\frac{1}{n{1+\lambda(x_i-\mu)}}, ]

where (\lambda) solves

[ \sum_i \frac{x_i-\mu}{1+\lambda(x_i-\mu)}=0. ]

The empirical likelihood-ratio statistic is

[ -2\log R(\mu)=2\sum_i\log{1+\lambda(x_i-\mu)}. ]

Under regularity conditions, this behaves asymptotically like (\chi^2_1), allowing a Wilks-style confidence set without assuming Normality.

In [42]:
def empirical_likelihood_mean_stat(x: np.ndarray, mu: float) -> float:
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    z = x - mu

    if mu <= x.min() or mu >= x.max():
        return np.inf
    if abs(z.mean()) < 1e-13:
        return 0.0

    # Feasible lambda interval from 1 + lambda*z_i > 0 for every i.
    pos = z[z > 0]
    neg = z[z < 0]
    lower = -1 / pos.max() if len(pos) else -np.inf
    upper = -1 / neg.min() if len(neg) else np.inf

    eps = 1e-12
    lo = lower + eps * max(1.0, abs(lower))
    hi = upper - eps * max(1.0, abs(upper))

    def score(lam):
        return np.sum(z / (1 + lam*z))

    sol = root_scalar(score, bracket=[lo, hi], method='brentq')
    lam = sol.root
    return float(2 * np.sum(np.log1p(lam*z)))

# Build a 95% empirical-likelihood confidence set for the Gentoo mean.
mu_grid = np.linspace(np.quantile(gentoo_mass, .05), np.quantile(gentoo_mass, .95), 450)
el_stat = np.array([empirical_likelihood_mean_stat(gentoo_mass, m) for m in mu_grid])
cutoff = stats.chi2.ppf(.95, df=1)
inside = mu_grid[el_stat <= cutoff]
el_ci = (inside.min(), inside.max())

normal_ci = stats.t.interval(.95, df=len(gentoo_mass)-1,
                             loc=gentoo_mass.mean(),
                             scale=gentoo_mass.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(gentoo_mass)))

pd.DataFrame({
    'method': ['empirical likelihood', 'classical t interval'],
    'lower_95': [el_ci[0], normal_ci[0]],
    'upper_95': [el_ci[1], normal_ci[1]],
    'point_estimate': [gentoo_mass.mean(), gentoo_mass.mean()]
})

           x_axis_label='hypothesized mean mu (g)',

What empirical likelihood adds conceptually¶

Bootstrap says:

Approximate repeated samples from the empirical distribution.

Empirical likelihood says:

Reweight the observed support points subject to moment constraints and build a likelihood-ratio statistic.

Both are nonparametric in spirit, but they attack inference from different directions.

12. One dataset, one conceptual chain¶

The most important outcome of ST4231 is seeing these methods as a connected toolkit rather than isolated formulas.

Statistical obstacle Computational response Penguin case-study example
Need draws from a non-Uniform distribution Inverse / rejection / transformation Exponential and Beta validation simulations
Population is a mixture Composition sampling Species-weighted body-mass generator
Need a difficult expectation Monte Carlo Tail probability under fitted mixture
Monte Carlo is noisy Antithetic / control variates Same target with less repeated-run variance
Interesting event is rare Importance sampling Extreme Gentoo body-mass tail
Component labels are hidden EM Recover 3 latent morphology clusters
Need samples from a target distribution Markov-chain design Stationary-distribution demonstration
Posterior known only up to proportionality Metropolis–Hastings Posterior Gentoo mean
Full conditionals are easy Gibbs sampling Joint posterior of mean and variance
Estimator sampling law is awkward Bootstrap Difference in species median body mass
Need cheaper local resampling Jackknife SE of Gentoo mean
Want likelihood-style nonparametric inference Empirical likelihood CI for Gentoo mean

13. Diagnostics and failure modes — the table to remember¶

Method Primary diagnostic Typical failure mode Practical response
Inverse transform Simulated vs theoretical moments/CDF Incorrect inverse or numerical endpoint problem Unit-test moments and quantiles
Rejection sampling Acceptance rate Loose envelope / invalid bound Improve proposal and verify (M)
Monte Carlo Monte Carlo SE / convergence Slow (1/\sqrt n) error reduction More samples or variance reduction
Antithetic variables Covariance / repeated-run variance Pairing does not induce useful negative dependence Check empirical variance before adopting
Control variates Correlation with target quantity Weak or badly estimated control Choose strongly correlated known-mean controls
Importance sampling Weight distribution, ESS Weight degeneracy / tail mismatch Redesign proposal; inspect log weights
EM Log-likelihood path, multi-start comparison Local optima / covariance collapse Multiple starts, regularization
Metropolis–Hastings Trace, ACF, ESS, acceptance Random-walk stickiness or rejection Tune proposal; reparameterize
Gibbs Trace, ACF, ESS Strong posterior coupling Blocking / reparameterization
Bootstrap Stability over B Wrong resampling unit / ignored dependence Match resampling scheme to data structure
Jackknife Agreement for smooth statistics Non-smooth estimator instability Prefer bootstrap or specialized theory
Empirical likelihood Feasibility / ratio curve Mean outside convex hull; numerical instability Respect constraint geometry and stable root solving

14. Complexity and scaling summary¶

Let:

  • (n): number of observations or simulation draws;
  • (d): feature dimension;
  • (K): mixture components;
  • (T): MCMC iterations;
  • (B): bootstrap replicates.
Method Approximate time complexity Scaling intuition
Inverse-transform draws (\Theta(n)) One transformation per draw
Rejection sampling (\Theta(n/a)) expected (a) = acceptance probability
Dense Cholesky (\Theta(d^3)) One-time covariance factorization
Multivariate draws after Cholesky (\Theta(nd^2)) Dense matrix-vector multiplication
Plain Monte Carlo (\Theta(n)) + function cost Precision improves only as (n^{-1/2})
Importance sampling (\Theta(n)) + density cost Weight stability matters more than raw n
EM, full covariance roughly (\Theta(nKd^2)) / iteration Repeated responsibility + covariance updates
Random-walk MH (\Theta(T,C_{target})) ESS can be far smaller than T
Gibbs (\Theta(T,C_{conditionals})) Depends on conditional sampling cost
Bootstrap (\Theta(B,C_{stat}(n))) Embarrassingly parallel in many cases
Jackknife (\Theta(n,C_{stat}(n))) naive Can be optimized for some statistics
Empirical likelihood grid root solve per candidate mean Numerical optimization dominates

Efficiency principle¶

A recurring theme across ST4231 is:

Do not count raw iterations; count useful information produced per unit computation.

Examples:

  • rejection sampler → accepted draws per proposal;
  • Monte Carlo → variance per function evaluation;
  • importance sampling → effective weighted sample size;
  • MCMC → ESS per iteration or per second;
  • bootstrap → stability of SE/CI as (B) increases.

15. Guided experiments for deeper understanding¶

These are deliberately phrased as experiments rather than formula exercises.

Experiment 1 — rejection sampling efficiency¶

Change the rejection envelope (M) to 1.2*M, 2*M, and 5*M.

Predict before running: what happens to acceptance probability? Does correctness change?

Experiment 2 — Monte Carlo error law¶

For (n\in{100, 400, 1600, 6400, 25600}), repeat the same Monte Carlo estimate hundreds of times and measure RMSE.

Check whether

[ RMSE\times\sqrt n ]

is approximately stable.

Experiment 3 — antithetic variables can fail to help¶

Replace (h(z)=e^z) with a function for which (h(z)) and (h(-z)) are positively correlated or nearly uncorrelated. Compare estimator variance.

Experiment 4 — importance-sampling proposal search¶

Vary the proposal mean and SD. Build a table with:

  • estimator variance;
  • weight ESS;
  • maximum log weight;
  • fraction of zero rare-event contributions.

Ask which metric best predicts reliability.

Experiment 5 — EM local optima¶

Increase the number of random starts from 12 to 100. Plot final log-likelihood by seed.

Ask whether the highest-likelihood clustering also gives the highest ARI against species.

Experiment 6 — MCMC tuning¶

Use proposal SDs from 1 g to 1500 g. Plot:

[ \text{acceptance rate} \quad\text{vs}\quad \text{ESS/1000 iterations}. ]

Find an example where a very high acceptance rate corresponds to poor ESS.

Experiment 7 — MCMC initialization stress test¶

Run four Metropolis chains from 3500, 4500, 5500, and 7000 g. Overlay trace plots.

How quickly do they forget the starting value?

Experiment 8 — bootstrap statistic choice¶

Repeat the bootstrap section for:

  • mean difference;
  • median difference;
  • ratio of means;
  • correlation between flipper length and body mass.

Which bootstrap distributions look symmetric? Which do not?

Experiment 9 — jackknife on a non-smooth statistic¶

Apply the jackknife to the median rather than the mean. Compare its SE with bootstrap SE.

This is a useful demonstration of why smoothness assumptions matter.

Experiment 10 — empirical likelihood geometry¶

Move the hypothesized mean outside the observed data range. Explain why the empirical-likelihood moment constraint cannot be satisfied with nonnegative probabilities.

16. Final conceptual recap¶

ST4231 can be condensed into a single philosophy:

[ \boxed{\text{When analytic statistics becomes difficult, design a stochastic or iterative computation whose behaviour you can justify and diagnose.}} ]

The algorithms differ, but the reasoning pattern is stable:

  1. identify the target quantity or target distribution;
  2. rewrite the problem into an expectation, latent-variable objective, resampling scheme, or stationary-distribution condition;
  3. design the algorithm;
  4. validate it where a known answer exists;
  5. measure computational uncertainty;
  6. diagnose efficiency rather than trusting raw iteration counts;
  7. stress-test tuning choices and failure modes;
  8. translate simulation output back into a statistical statement.

The deepest connections¶

  • Monte Carlo: integration (\leftrightarrow) averaging.
  • Variance reduction: estimator design (\leftrightarrow) computational efficiency.
  • EM: missing labels (\leftrightarrow) expected complete-data likelihood.
  • MCMC: difficult target density (\leftrightarrow) stationary distribution of a designed chain.
  • Bootstrap: unknown sampling distribution (\leftrightarrow) resampling from the empirical distribution.
  • Empirical likelihood: moment constraints (\leftrightarrow) nonparametric likelihood ratios.

If you understand those transformations rather than only memorizing algorithm steps, you have understood the central intellectual purpose of computer-intensive statistical methods.

Data¶

Software used¶

  • pandas — tables and data manipulation
  • scikit-learn — Adjusted Rand Index only; EM itself is implemented from scratch
  • Bokeh — all plots

Reproducibility¶

Most stochastic sections use deterministic seeds derived from RANDOM_SEED = 4231. Exact floating-point results can still vary slightly across library versions, but statistical conclusions should remain stable.
